abstract: Derived characters that may have emerged via positive selection can be identified by comparing species, but also possibly subgroups within species. Allopatric and sympatric polymorphism observed in many salmonids is thought to emerge mainly in landlocked populations, which have lost the anadromous lifestyle of their ancestors. Populations of Arctic charr (Salvelinus alpinus) are an example of such polymorphism, commonly diverging along a pelagic-benthic axis. Populations of Icelandic charr can be anadromous or landlocked, like in Lake Thingvallavatn where four morphs coexist differing in habitat use, preferred prey and external feeding morphology. Three of these morphs are also caught in the neighboring Lake Ulfljotsvatn, despite prey availability in the two lakes differing notably. We studied variation of craniofacial morphology in Icelandic charr populations and compared the ecologically specialized sympatric morphs to five anadromous charr populations and to two non-specialized lake populations, as well as across two connected lakes. The results indicate minor variation among anadromous populations and that the benthic lake forms are derived. There was clear phenotypic difference between benthic and pelagic morphs within Thingvallavatn but no differences between the morphs in Ulfljotsvatn. Patterns of variation between corresponding morphs across the two lakes suggest genetics separation and phenotypic plasticity.
